newsitem.title: USA: New products - Flavored milk, trivia-brainteaser games.
newsitem.headline: New products - Flavored milk, trivia-brainteaser games.

text.p: A new line of beverages hopes to make milk the drink of chice for pre-teens and their parents, pushing soft drinks and bottled beverages out of the lunch box.

Smilk is a new line of fruit-flavored, non-fat milk drinks, currently available in such kid-friendly varieties as raspberry jazz, orange vanilla, pleasin' punch, chuggin' cherry, grinnin' grape, tropicow and veryvery strawberry. The drinks contain natural and artificial flavors, a spokeswoman for Smilk said.

An eight-ounce serving of Smilk contains about 275 mgs. of calcium, approximately 30 percent of a child's recommended daily intake. It also contains about 25 percent of a daily requirement of vitamin D. This serving has 24 grams of sugar, the sweeteners being a company secret, and 130 calories.
The milk drinks are fat free, do not contain aspertame, and must be refrigerated.

The makers of Smilk hope to appeal to the 97 percent of kids under age 13 who are milk drinkers. These young people are the highest per capita milk consumers, drinking an average of 26.3 gallons each, on an annual basis. However, given the 800 mg. per day recommended minimum for calcium intake for children, they should be drinking 80 gallons a year, Smilk says.
Flavored milk, such as pre-packaged chocolate or strawberry flavored milk drinks by Hershey, currently account for about 4.5 percent of total milk sales.

In general, milk consumption has been declining, from 24 gallons per capita in 1964 to 19 gallons per capita in 1993. By the same token, soft drink consumption has been rising, up to 48 gallons per capita in the United States in 1993 from 17 gallons per capita in 1964. In all, kids drink about $5 billion worth of soft drinks, and teens nationwide drink about $10 billion worth, Smilk says.
Smilk is currently available in Michigan and Ohio, will be rolled out nationally in the near future.
It comes in 1/2 pints, ranging in price from 39 cents to 49 cents; pints at 79 cents to 99 cents and quarts at $1.39 to $1.49.

Smilk, based in Greenwich, Conn., said that the drinks are produced and distributed by Country Fresh Inc, of Grand Rapids, Mich. Discussions are under way with other potential dairy licensees across the country.
For more information, call 1-888-GO SMILK (467-6455).

For kids and kids at heart, Cardinal Industries, a Long Island, N.Y.-based toy maker, has developed the Nick at Nite Classic TV Trivia Game. It tests tv knowledge, based on classic tv cable station, Nick at Nite.
It contains questions such as -- How much did an episode of "Mr. Ed" cost ($55,000) -- or -- How many Emmy awards did Sally Field win as star of "The Flying Nun?" (none).

The game has some 3,000 trivia questions, which range in difficulty from "rookie" to "fanatic." Players have to answer questions correctly in order to get pieces of the special Nick at Nite tv dinner puzzle. Players also get to act out their favourite classic tv stars, such as Laura Petrie on "The Dick Van Dyke Show" or Latka on "Taxi".
The game, which costs about $19.99, is recommended for ages eight and up. It is being introduced nationally.
Question: Forward, I'm heavy, backward I'm not. What am I?
Answer: I'm the word "ton."
Sounds simple? This and 500 increasingly difficult riddles, puzzles, mysteries, conundrums and trick questions comprise Mindtrap, a game newly introduced into the United States by Pressman Toy Corp.
The game, popular in Canada, requires skills of logic and deduction to solve puzzles.
Question: What is the closest relation that your father's sister's sister-in-law could be to you?
Answer: Your mother.
The game requires two players or two teams. It's recommended for ages 12 and up. It costs about $19.95.
New York-based Pressman can be contacted by calling 212-675-7910 for more information.
